evidence.quote: The route runs along the base of the Warner Mountains in northeastern California and encompasses stretches of roadway in Nevada.

evidence.claim: Pavement gives way to improved gravel and dirt; the Bureau of Land Management advises allowing at least three hours.

evidence.claim: BLM presents its Back Country Byways as opportunities to learn the natural and cultural history of these landscapes.
evidence.quote: The Bureau of Land Management established Back Country Byways, part of the National Scenic Byways network, to provide recreational and educational opportunities

evidence.claim: West of Mosquito Valley, the road narrows and climbs a fairly steep grade, a distinct change from the flat basin floors.
evidence.quote: The road west out of Mosquito Valley is narrow and fairly steep

evidence.claim: The corridor crosses an older route: the Applegate-Lassen Trail carried emigrants through Surprise Valley in the 1840s and 1850s.
evidence.quote: Emigrants traveling the Applegate-Lassen trail passed through Surprise Valley in the 1840s and 1850s on their way to California and Oregon.

evidence.claim: Many emigrant trails followed routes already used by American Indians, and passing livestock depleted forage and frightened away game on which local tribes depended.
evidence.quote: Many of the early emigrant trails followed trails created and used by American Indians. The emigrants and their livestock depleted the forage along the trails, scared off wild game that the local tribes depended on

evidence.claim: Settlers later homesteaded on Northern Paiute winter villages at the northern end of the valley.
evidence.quote: The earliest settlers homesteaded at the northern end of the valley on the winter villages of the Northern Paiute.

evidence.claim: The Enlarged Homestead Act of 1909 doubled claims from 160 to 320 acres; Long and Mosquito valleys later lost more than forty homesteading families.
evidence.quote: The Enlarged Homestead Act of 1909 increased the amount of land homesteaders could claim from 160 acres to 320 acres.

evidence.claim: Settlement at the north end of Surprise Valley brought settlers onto Northern Paiute winter village sites.
evidence.quote: The earliest settlers homesteaded at the northern end of the valley on the winter villages of the Northern Paiute.

evidence.claim: As tensions increased, settlers petitioned for troops, and a military fort was established.
evidence.quote: As tension between the settlers and the Northern Paiute increased, the settlers petitioned Unidentified man with dog in Surprise Valley the government to send Army circa 1885 troops for protection. A military fort was established

evidence.claim: The BLM guide records the conversion of its buildings into a regional Indian school and hospital in 1892.
evidence.quote: In 1892, the Army presence was no longer needed and the buildings were turned into a regional Indian school and hospital.

evidence.claim: The Fort Bidwell Indian Reservation and Cedarville Rancheria remain homes to Northern Paiute people.
evidence.quote: The Fort Bidwell Indian Reservation in Fort Bidwell and the Cedarville Rancheria in Cedarville continue to be the home to many Northern Paiute.

evidence.claim: In town, the guide identifies the community church and Kober’s Drygoods among buildings retaining their century-old appearance.
evidence.quote: Historic buildings such as the Fort Bidwell Hotel, Kober’s Drygoods (pictured above) and the community church still look as they did over 100 years ago.

evidence.claim: The General Store was built of stone in 1874 to resist fire, a material choice made when this was a remote outpost.
evidence.quote: In order to be fire-proof, it was constructed from stone and when it was built in 1874 this was truly an outpost in the Wild West.

evidence.claim: The byway crosses Mosquito Lake on a levee, with water possible in spring and early summer.
evidence.quote: As you drive on the levee over Mosquito Lake, you may see water in the spring and early summer.

evidence.claim: That intermittent water provides migrating birds with food and protection: water and mud deter predators.
evidence.quote: Intermittent lakes are lifesavers for migrating birds because there is plenty of food and predators are deterred by the water and mud.

evidence.claim: The BLM guide singles out shorebirds with long legs and pointed or curved bills, including willets whose flight reveals a black-and-white pattern.
evidence.quote: Mosquito Lake is particularly popular with shore birds that are characterized by their long legs, pointed and sometimes curved beaks. If a flock of birds flies by you displaying a striking black and white pattern you are looking at a flock of willets.

evidence.claim: The surrounding uplands hold another source of water: springs fed by melting winter snow supply moisture even in late summer.
evidence.quote: As elevation increases on the surrounding uplands, springs fed by the melted winter snowpack provide water even in the late summer.

evidence.claim: At the guide’s Basin and Range stop, a short dirt road to the southeast provides a view back toward Mosquito Lake and the mountains beyond.
evidence.quote: A short (0.1 mile) drive or walk down the dirt road to the southeast provides a lovely view of Mosquito Lake and the mountains beyond.

evidence.claim: BLM advises against long trailers and long motor homes on the narrow, fairly steep road west out of Mosquito Valley.
evidence.quote: The road west out of Mosquito Valley is narrow and fairly steep and not recommended for long trailers and long motor homes.

evidence.claim: Dirt sections of the byway require high ground clearance and possibly four-wheel drive.
evidence.quote: Still other sections have a dirt surface that will require a vehicle with high ground clearance and possibly four-wheel drive.

evidence.claim: Fortynine Rock marked a water stop on the Applegate-Lassen Trail, one of the routes used during the California gold rush of 1849.
evidence.quote: You are now on the Applegate- Lassen Trail, one of the routes of the 1849 California gold rush.

evidence.claim: The first “49” marking is said to have been applied with wagon axle grease, an account recorded in the BLM guide.
evidence.quote: the first “49” marking on Fortynine Rock is said to have been put on with wagon axle grease.

evidence.claim: Emigrants used that material to record initials or the year of their passage on rocks.
evidence.quote: Pioneers often used axle grease to sign rocks with their initials or the year they passed through.

evidence.claim: Here the mark identified Fortynine Camp, the last campsite with good water before the dry floor of Surprise Valley.
evidence.quote: For the pioneers, this rock marked Fortynine Camp and was the last place to camp with good water before crossing the dry Henry Lind’s 1941 photo of 49 Rock basin floor of Surprise Valley.

evidence.claim: The guide also describes emigrants crossing Fortynine Lake as they traveled west through this country, with the lake normally dry in late summer and fall.
evidence.quote: The weary 49ers came straight west across the valley and Fortynine Lake below you. In late summer and fall the lake was normally dry
